About Mokoro Journeys: private, low-impact safaris in Botswana.
Clouds over open savanna just before sunset
A mokoro is the dugout canoe poled through the channels of the Okavango Delta. It is slow, silent and leaves no trace, which is how we think a safari should feel.
We plan private safaris in Botswana for people who would rather have a quiet camp than a big lodge.

That usually means fly-in camps in private concessions, a mix of water and dry country, and enough time in each place to slow down. We follow the idea behind Botswana's "high value, low volume" tourism: fewer visitors, less impact, more of the income staying in the country.
We tell you what a month is good for and what it is not, including when we think you should go somewhere else.
We choose camps by how they manage sightings, not by how they look in brochures.
Guides, polers and staff from Botswana, and camps that share income with neighbouring communities.
No invented reviews, no awards we have not won. Ask us for references and we will put you in touch with past travellers who have agreed to talk.

How the Mokoro Journeys website uses cookies and browser storage.
What cookies and local storage are

Cookies are small text files a website saves in your browser. Local storage is a similar feature that lets a website remember information on your own device. Neither is sent to us unless a page specifically reads it.
This website does not set any cookies, and it does not use advertising or tracking cookies of any kind.
This website does not use local storage.

We do not use analytics, advertising or social-media tracking on this website. Photographs are loaded from our image delivery provider, which receives the standard technical information (such as your IP address) that any website receives when it delivers an image; it does not set cookies through these images. Fonts are served from our own website.
Consent and how to withdraw it

Because this website sets no cookies and stores nothing in your browser, there is nothing to consent to and no cookie banner. If that ever changes, we will ask for your consent first and you will be able to change your choice at any time.

You can clear anything a website has stored in your browser at any time by clearing its site data (usually under Settings, then Privacy, then Cookies and site data), or block cookies entirely in your browser settings. This website will work exactly the same.

The Central Kalahari Game Reserve is semi-desert, not sand dunes: grass and scrub on deep sand, cut by ancient dry river valleys such as Deception Valley. After the summer rains the valleys fill with springbok, gemsbok and their predators.

It is also the ancestral land of the San and Bakgalagadi peoples, whose rights to live in the reserve have been a matter of national debate and court cases. We include this history on visits rather than leaving it out.

The northern edge of Chobe National Park follows the Chobe River near Kasane. In the dry months, when the inland pans have gone, elephants and buffalo walk to the river in large numbers in the afternoon.
It is also the busiest part of any Botswana park. Our approach is to keep time here short, use small boats rather than large launches, and go out at quieter times of day.

The Linyanti flows along the border with Namibia's Zambezi region and spreads into a swamp of reeds and lagoons. Behind it is dry mopane woodland, so in the dry months the river is the only water for a long way, and wildlife comes to it.
The area is divided into private concessions with a few small camps each. That means off-road driving to follow sightings, night drives and walking, all with a very small number of guests.

The Makgadikgadi is the bed of a vast ancient lake. Most of the year the pans are white crust under a huge sky; after good summer rain, the grasslands at their edges turn green and thousands of zebra and wildebeest move in.
In the dry season the zebra move west to the Boteti River, and the pans become a place for silence, sleep-outs under the stars and walks with Zu/'hoasi San guides in some areas.

Moremi was set aside in the 1960s at the initiative of the local Batawana community and is named after their chief, Moremi III. It covers a large part of the eastern Delta, including Chief's Island, and mixes permanent water with dry land, so it works in more months than a purely water-based area.

Because Moremi is a public reserve, it sees more vehicles than a private concession, and park rules apply: no off-road driving and no night drives. We use it carefully, often staying in the private areas on its edges (such as Khwai) and visiting the reserve by day.

Nxai Pan National Park sits just north of the Makgadikgadi Pans National Park; the two parks border each other and are often visited together. Its pans are grassed rather than salt, so after the summer rains they fill with grazers and the cats that follow them.
At its southern edge stand Baines' Baobabs, a group of very old trees painted by Thomas Baines in 1862 and still recognisable today.

The Okavango River rises in the Angolan highlands and never reaches the sea. Rain that fell months earlier and hundreds of kilometres away spreads slowly across the Kalahari sand and fills the Delta just as the rest of Botswana is drying out. That timing is the reason a winter safari here looks the way it does: open water, green islands and wildlife that has walked in from the dry country.

Most of the Delta is divided into large private concessions, each with a handful of small camps. That is where the low-volume model is most visible: you can spend a morning in a mokoro and not see another boat.
In 2014 the Okavango Delta became the 1,000th site inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List.

The Savute Channel links the Linyanti system to the Savuti Marsh. For long periods it has run dry, then flowed again; when it carries water the whole area changes. Around it are open grasslands, rocky hills with San rock paintings and long-standing territories of lion and hyena.
Savuti is part of Chobe National Park, so park rules apply, but it is far enough from Kasane and Maun that it feels much quieter than the riverfront.

Four quartzite hills rise from the flat sand of north-west Botswana. They hold a very large concentration of rock art and have been a place of spiritual importance for a very long time. They have been called the "Louvre of the Desert", a phrase quoted in UNESCO's World Heritage listing, and in 2001 became Botswana's first World Heritage Site.
This is a cultural visit rather than a wildlife one. We pair it with the Okavango Panhandle, where the river enters Botswana.

High value, low volume: why Botswana keeps its camps small | Mokoro Journeys

Many safari countries grew tourism by adding beds. Botswana, from the 1990s onwards, chose a different path in its national tourism policy: fewer visitors, higher prices and smaller footprints, especially in the most sensitive areas such as the Okavango Delta.
What it looks like in practice
Large wildlife areas are divided into concessions, each leased to an operator with a limit on beds.
Camps are often tented and built on raised decks so they can be removed.
Access is mostly by light aircraft, so there are fewer roads and fewer vehicles.
In private concessions, guides can drive off-road to follow a sighting, run night drives and lead walks, because there are so few vehicles.

The model is expensive for visitors, and it has been criticised for keeping local people and lower-budget travellers out. Community-based concessions, where villages lease their land to operators and share the income, are one answer. When we choose camps, we ask how much stays in Botswana: staff, ownership, community fees.
The policy is also changing. A revised national tourism policy in 2021 aims to widen access and diversify beyond the high-value model, so expect more variety in the years ahead.
For a traveller, the result is simple to describe: quiet. You might share a sighting with one other vehicle, or none.

Mokoro etiquette: a quiet way to travel
Sit low, keep still, keep your hands in the boat. What to expect on your first mokoro trip.
Mokoro etiquette: a quiet way to travel | Mokoro Journeys

A mokoro (plural: mekoro) was traditionally carved from a single tree trunk. Today, most mekoro used in tourism are made of fibreglass, which saves trees and lasts longer. Your guide, known as a poler, stands at the back and pushes the boat through the shallow channels with a long pole called a ngashi.
Sit low and keep still. Mekoro are narrow and easy to tip.
Keep your hands inside the boat. The water is shallow but home to crocodiles and hippos.
Speak quietly and follow your poler's directions.
Bring a hat and sunscreen; there is no shade.

Mokoro trips are less about big animals and more about detail: painted reed frogs on papyrus stems, water lilies, jacanas walking on leaves, the sound of the pole. Most trips include a stop on an island for a short walk with your guide.

A soft bag with no wheels and no rigid frame, so it can be squeezed into the pod.

Extra weight can sometimes be carried by buying an extra seat, if booked in advance.
Three or four shirts in neutral colours (khaki, olive, sand), which stand out less on walks and in a mokoro.
Two pairs of trousers, one pair of shorts.
A warm fleece and a light down jacket for winter mornings (June to August).
A hat, sunglasses, sunscreen and a light scarf against dust.
Comfortable closed shoes for walks; sandals for camp.
Binoculars, one camera body and a zoom lens.
A small headlamp, medication and copies of documents.

Reading the flood: why the Delta is full in the dry season | Mokoro Journeys

The Okavango is often called a flood that arrives in the dry season. The reason is distance and gradient. Rain falls on the Angolan highlands from about November to March. The water flows down the Cubango and Cuito rivers into Namibia and then Botswana, and then spreads very slowly across an almost flat fan of sand.
March to April: the flood peaks in the Panhandle in the north-west.
May to June: it reaches the central Delta and spreads across the floodplains.
July to August: high water usually reaches the lower Delta and Maun.
September to November: the water recedes as heat and evaporation increase.

Each year is different. A big rain year in Angola can mean a large flood; a dry year can mean some channels never fill. Local rain in Botswana, from November to March, adds a second, smaller pulse of water.
For planning, this is why our month chooser shows two separate lines: water in the Delta, and green grass on the pans. They peak at opposite times of year.

Botswana month by month: when the Okavango floods, when the pans turn green, and what each month is good for.
Botswana works all year, but not in the same places. Choose a month to see where to go.

Rain falls on the highlands of Angola from about November to March. It takes months to travel down the Okavango River and spread across the almost flat Delta. So the water arrives in the central Delta around May and June and is usually highest from June to August, just as the rest of Botswana dries out. Wildlife walks in from the dry country to the permanent water.

The Makgadikgadi, Nxai Pan and the Central Kalahari have little permanent water. When the summer rains come, from about November or December, grass grows fast and zebra, wildebeest, springbok and gemsbok move in to graze and give birth. Predators follow. It is the green season: hot, stormy, beautiful and quieter in many camps.
Typical patterns, not forecasts. Flood size and timing change each year with rainfall in Angola, and local rains vary.
